evidence.title: Informal use of generative artificial intelligence by nursing interns during clinical placement: A multi-stakeholder interpretive description
evidence.outcome: Presence of institutional AI rules governing intern use during placement
evidence.effect: Theme 1 identified multilevel discretionary rule-making in a policy vacuum, with a cross-stakeholder call for institutional frameworks.
evidence.quote: Five interconnected themes emerged: (1) multilevel discretionary rule-making in a policy vacuum; (2) a universally endorsed but unevenly enacted verification imperative; (3) intuitive risk stratification; (4) tensions between standardised AI outputs and embodied nursing care; and (5) a cross-stakeholder call for institutional frameworks.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (nursing interns, preceptors, head nurses, administrators, IT specialists, quality officer)

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether a written, leadership-approved AI policy reduces inconsistent or outdated rules for AI use, so the recommendation rests on 11 endorsements and seven studies showing that such policies are often absent. In five surveys, between 4.8% and 37.6% of respondents reported a formal institutional AI policy or guidance, while AI use was reported far more often.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations with and without a written AI policy on any outcome. The seven hazard studies are six level 3 surveys and one qualitative study of self-reported policy presence. They establish a governance gap, but they cannot show that writing, versioning, or disseminating a policy changes staff behavior or patient outcomes.

In the Türkiye survey, 87% of hematologists reported clinical AI use in the prior three months while 4.8% reported a written policy. In Latin America, 78.3% of respondents used generative AI and 7.4% reported policies. These figures suggest AI reaches care without institutional rules, but no study shows a policy catches errors before they reach patients.

Interviews with 32 nursing interns, preceptors, administrators, and IT staff in China described multilevel discretionary rule-making in a policy vacuum, and stakeholders asked for institutional frameworks. This suggests that units write their own rules when no policy exists. No study measured whether a written policy is read, followed, or kept current in daily work.

One survey drew 123 emergency clinicians from 16 Latin American countries in non-English settings and found that 7.4% reported institutional AI policies. No study sampled Medicaid or safety-net organizations. None examined whether institutional policies address equitable use, language access, or health literacy for patients.

FDA draft guidance expects device manufacturers to review their quality systems at defined intervals. California AB 3030 requires disclosure of GenAI patient communications unless a licensed clinician reviews them. A written policy could record how a health system meets such duties, but these sources set obligations and do not test health-system policies.

Among 109 family medicine chairs, 56.9% reported current AI use and 37.6% reported formal written policies, strategic plans, or frameworks. In the UK sample, 11% reported institutional guidance. Many departments appear to adopt AI before governance exists. No study reports the staff time or cost of drafting, versioning, and disseminating a policy.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations with and without a leadership-approved, versioned AI policy on outcomes such as the share of AI tools that pass approval review, the rate of unsanctioned tool use, staff awareness of the rules, or reported AI-related safety events. A before-and-after or stepped rollout study across several health systems, including safety-net sites, could address this gap. It would need to measure policy awareness, adherence, and whether reviews happen on schedule.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard survey sampled clinicians in non-English settings in Latin America and shows that the policy gap exists there. It offers no evidence on whether a written policy would work in under-resourced settings or protect patients with limited English or low literacy.
